slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open by asking what structure a projective plane must have beyond incidence. Chapter 5 built the real projective plane from coordinates. This chapter asks which incidence configurations force a plane to be coordinatizable by a field and which configurations can fail, leading to exotic non-Desarguesian planes. Orient students to printed pages 117 through 142.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the four themes: the Pappus configuration as a test for commutativity, the Desargues configuration as a test for associativity and the existence of coordinates from a division ring, the Moulton plane as a counterexample where Desargues fails, and projective arithmetic that recovers field operations from pure incidence.

slides.label: Pappus
slides.narration: Present Pappus theorem: if points A B C are collinear and D E F are collinear, then the three cross-join intersection points are also collinear. This theorem holds in every projective plane coordinatized by a commutative field and fails in planes over non-commutative division rings.

slides.label: Desargues
slides.narration: Present Desargues theorem: if two triangles are in perspective from a point, then they are in perspective from a line and conversely. This theorem holds in every projective plane that can be embedded in three-dimensional projective space, and it is equivalent to coordinatizability by a division ring.

slides.label: Moulton Plane
slides.narration: Show the Moulton plane as a concrete counterexample. In the Moulton plane, lines with negative slope that cross the y-axis are bent at the axis. The incidence axioms still hold, but the Desargues configuration fails because the three intersection points are no longer collinear.

slides.label: Projective Arithmetic
slides.narration: Explain how to recover field operations from incidence alone. Addition is defined by a ruler-and-pencil construction using parallel lines and a unit point. Multiplication uses a similar triangle configuration. The resulting operations satisfy the field axioms precisely when Pappus theorem holds.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter by connecting Pappus, Desargues, the Moulton counterexample, and projective arithmetic into a single narrative. The key lesson is that geometry and algebra are two views of the same structure: incidence configurations determine and are determined by the algebraic properties of the coordinate system.
